articles.title: ‘We live in grief-phobic societies’: experts on how to get more comfortable with death
articles.summary: We are all going to die, and so is everyone we know. So how can you not be terrified? For most people, death is not a standard conversation topic. Once, at lunch, a friend began talking about her mother’s death several years earlier.
body: Afterwards, I asked him what was wrong. “I really don’t like talking about death,” he said, his hands twitching anxiously. “I don’t even like thinking about it. It freaks me out.”
His discomfort struck me as silly – and also the most normal thing in the world. We are all going to die, and so is everyone we know. So why be terrified? And how can you not be terrified?

My friend is far from alone in his discomfort. “We live in grief-illiterate and grief-phobic societies,” says Dr Lucy Hone, a resilience and grief researcher and author of the book How Will I Get Ever Through This?: A Practical Guide to Navigating Life’s Toughest Times.

Hone began researching grief over a decade ago, after the sudden death of her daughter, Abi. On our video call, she wears one of Abi’s old hats, an orange and white beanie with polka dots and a big orange pouf on top. It’s ridiculous, Hone says, but it makes her laugh.

articles.title: Alice Zaslavsky’s shortcut beetroot baked risotto – recipe
articles.summary: An unconventional technique makes this vibrant rice – finished with dill fronds – a lower-touch dinner for weeknights. Check out more Alice Zaslavsky recipes. This shortcut risotto will have purists shaking their fists, but I like to live dangerously.
body: Use a microplane to grate the parmesan over the risotto. This will yield a cloud-like consistency, but you could also just blitz the parmesan to a crumb in the food processor before grating the veg. I’d avoid buying pre‑grated parmesan, as it’s kept crumby with anti-caking agent, and the aroma is … not great.
For extra flavour, use vegetable or chicken stock instead of water. And if you have herbs growing in the garden, some parsley, chives or even chervil won’t go astray.
Grate the veg Grate the onion and beetroot using a box grater or the coarsest setting of your food processor. Chop up any chunkier bits.

Start your base Glug the olive oil and half the butter into a shallow flameproof casserole dish over medium heat. Dump in the grated veg and the garlic and stir about until you hear a sizzle. Whack the lid on and set the timer for six minutes, stirring halfway. Meanwhile, bring a kettle of water to the boil.

articles.title: The Fine Dining Flip
articles.summary: When Chateau Royale opened in New York City last year, it embodied the city’s rising “swankstaurant” moment, in which the saturation of the steakhouse gave rise to “a new age of gloss,” per Grub Street’s Matthew Schneier.
body: Over the past few months, Pruitt and his business partner Jacob Cohen have done two shake-ups like this, in an almost too-on-the-nose manifestation of the current economic climate. In June, they replaced their French bistro Libertine, where duck for two clocked in at $72 in 2023, with Capitaine, where — excluding the caviar and seafood towers — the highest-priced item on the menu is the $52 steak frites. Most dishes are under $30, with more snacks on the menu to allow diners lower-key ways of stopping in — there are only so many special occasion spots a city can sustain.

“At a certain point, the world around both [restaurants] began to change,” Pruitt says. “We were increasingly conscious of what a restaurant costs people and how often they could use it.” There is a difference, he notes, between a restaurant that belongs to a neighborhood and one that merely takes up space in it.

For the owners of some high-end restaurants, the current economic landscape has led to an existential pondering. Does everyone really want near-$100 shareable mains, especially on the average weeknight? What’s the point of the luxurious, glitzy restaurant to which many diners might go only once or twice?

articles.title: Princess Lilibet Makes Jam (and Memories) With Mom Meghan Markle in a New Home Video
articles.summary: The Duchess of Sussex shared a new video with her five-year-old daughter—and a rare glimpse of Lilibet’s voice—to celebrate her brand, As Ever.
body: On Tuesday, the Duchess of Sussex shared a new video on Instagram to celebrate the brand’s holiday collection. The video is a sweet mashup of clips showing the Duchess’s journey from a young entrepreneur to starting her own brand in 2025 and seeing it through different chapters.

One clip gives a rare glimpse into the family’s life at home, with the Duchess and Princess Lilibet in the kitchen making one of the brand’s signature offerings—raspberry jam. Meghan shows a pot of berries boiling on the stove, and pans over to little Lilibet, wooden spoon in hand. “What do you think, Lily?” Meghan asks. “I think it’s beautiful,” the princess replies.
Meghan went on to thank her As Ever team. “As I pinch myself looking at how this brand has grown, and as we introduce our holiday collection, I feel very proud, and grateful,” she wrote.

Attendees gathered for an evening of conversation with evolutionary scholar and author Dr. Cat Bohannon, Kloss, and U.N. Goodwill Ambassador and ACLU artist ambassador Padma Lakshmi.

articles.title: On the Podcast: Haider Ackermann’s Tom Ford Is About Risk and Freedom
articles.summary: A few days after presenting his spring 2027 collection for Tom Ford, Haider Ackermann sat down with Nicole Phelps in his Paris office to discuss his latest show, his inspirations, and how he became a fashion designer on “The Run-Through.”
body: They began by talking about desire and seduction. “We’re living in a period where men are more vain than they have ever been before,” Ackermann told Nicole. “And they’re embracing their feminine side. They’re more daring.” He encouraged his models to seduce the crowd and to feel joy as they stalked the runway. He also insisted that the point of all that sexiness wasn’t merely to provoke. “I am interested in taking risks and feeling free, certainly in a world where everything is more puritan and reserved,” he said.

When Nicole noted the dedicated group of friends and customers who go to all of Ackermann’s shows—Tilda Swinton among them—he replied: “I do believe in loyalty. I’m very loyal to all my exes. I don’t know how to dis-love once I have loved.”

Ackermann will soon be off to Chile to go kayaking amid the glaciers. He travels all around the globe, but has a particular affinity for remote places where his cellphone has no service. “It is perhaps in search of silence. When you go very far away and lose yourself and feel so small against Mother Nature, you’re suddenly much closer to yourself,” he reflected.
